blueprint_topic: Management of Care — goals-of-care support, surrogate communication, client advocacy, and uncertainty-aware neuroprognostication after moderate-severe TBI
stem: A client with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury lacks decision-making capacity. Early in the ICU course, the family asks whether life-sustaining treatment should be limited because recovery is uncertain. Which nursing approach best supports appropriate goals-of-care decision-making?

options.A: Support clinician-surrogate discussion that acknowledges uncertainty, considers all available evidence, and centers the client's known values and prior wishes.
options.B: Use the admission neurologic findings and imaging as the main basis for an early treatment-limitation recommendation when the family asks for a clear answer.
options.C: Focus the discussion on predicted functional outcome and the clinical team's recommendation, adding the client's prior values after the prognosis becomes more certain.
options.D: Delay asking about the client's prior wishes until a prognostic model gives a stable outcome estimate, so preferences do not influence early clinical interpretation.

rationale: A is correct. The current Neurocritical Care Society guideline for neuroprognostication after moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury is specifically intended to support counseling of families and surrogate decision-makers. Its good-practice statements recommend that prognostication consider the complete clinical condition rather than a single variable, not be based only on ultra-early injury characteristics in the first 3 days, and be performed carefully with acknowledgment of uncertainty, without nihilism, and using all available evidence. The guideline also states that patient values and preferences are central to surrogate discussions and that shared decision-making based on careful prognostication is critical for treatment and goals-of-care decisions. NCSBN places advocacy, client rights, advance-care preferences, interdisciplinary communication, and Management of Care coordination within RN responsibilities. B is incorrect because admission findings and imaging alone should not drive premature treatment limitation. C is incorrect because the client's known values should not be treated as secondary information to be added only after prognosis becomes more certain. D is incorrect because patient preferences are central to goals-of-care discussion and should not be intentionally withheld from the decision process while waiting for a prediction model.
educational_objective: Support surrogate goals-of-care decisions after moderate-severe TBI by communicating prognostic uncertainty honestly, avoiding premature nihilism, using all available clinical evidence, and centering the client's known values and prior wishes.
source_organization: Neurocritical Care Society (NCS); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Guidelines for Neuroprognostication in Critically Ill Adults with Moderate–Severe Traumatic Brain Injury; Neurocritical Care Guidelines; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: NCS evidence-based guideline published/released February 2024 and still listed in the current NCS guideline library when rechecked 2026-08-20; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: Current NCS guideline library lists 'Guidelines for Neuroprognostication in Critically Ill Adults With Moderate–Severe Traumatic Brain Injury'; NCS release listing identifies February 2024. Official guideline, Good Practice Statements: (1) prognostication should consider the complete clinical condition and not a single variable; (2) prognostication should not be based only on ultra-early injury characteristics in the first 3 days and, unless irreversible brain-stem damage/imminent death or documented predetermined wishes apply, recommends a period of full support before definitive neuroprognostication; (3) prognostication should acknowledge uncertainty, avoid nihilism, and consider all available evidence rather than anecdote alone. Evidence-to-recommendation 'Balance of desirable and undesirable consequences' states that values/preferences are central to discussions with surrogates, goal-concordant decisions should align with perceived patient wishes, and shared decision-making based on careful prognostication is critical. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Management of Care supports client advocacy/rights, advance directives/preferences, multidisciplinary communication, and care coordination.
source_claim_supported: Fresh current NCS evidence directly supports uncertainty-aware, non-nihilistic neuroprognostication using all available evidence rather than ultra-early findings alone and explicitly centers patient values/preferences in surrogate goals-of-care decisions. NCSBN supports the RN advocacy and communication role; the item does not assign the nurse responsibility for independently determining neurologic prognosis or treatment withdrawal.
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: protect client rights and autonomy, integrate advance directives/preferences into care, advocate for the client, communicate with interdisciplinary team members, and coordinate care decisions.
pdf_visual_verification: NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan printed page 7 / PDF pageno 10 was freshly screenshot-verified earlier in this continuation on 2026-08-20. NCS clinical evidence for Q1975 is current HTML/open-access full text; no new PDF evidence is used.
correction_summary: Original Q1975 had a 175-character correct answer and substantially shorter distractors, with alternatives that made premature nihilism too easy to reject. The item was rebuilt so all four choices are plausible communication/decision-support strategies. The final key keeps the nurse in an advocacy/support role, explicitly respects prognostic uncertainty and patient values, and avoids making a universal legal claim about surrogate authority or assigning the nurse independent prognostic responsibility.

option_audit.A: Correct; integrates uncertainty, all available evidence, and the client's known values in clinician-surrogate shared decision support.
option_audit.B: Plausible early-clarity shortcut; incorrect because ultra-early admission findings/imaging alone should not drive treatment limitation.
option_audit.C: Plausible clinician-centered counseling approach; incorrect because patient values/preferences are central rather than secondary to prognosis.
option_audit.D: Plausible anti-bias approach; incorrect because intentionally withholding known patient wishes while awaiting a prediction model conflicts with value-concordant shared decision-making.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on all/only/always/never/must-type absolute wording.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths: A 159, B 157, C 167, D 165 characters; the correct answer is not the longest and choices are tightly balanced.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives are realistic counseling/decision-support approaches and differ in timing, evidentiary breadth, and role of client preferences.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified in the pre-stage audit. B overweights ultra-early evidence, C improperly subordinates patient values, and D wrongly delays elicitation/use of preferences. Post-fetch adversarial reread remains required.
